title: Selling eggs at the farm gate
subtitle: What small-scale registered producers need to do in England.
excerpt: Selling eggs from the farm gate is one of the simplest ways to cover the feed costs of a laying flock. In England, flocks of fewer than 50 hens can sell direct to the final consumer at the farm gate or local markets without grading, but there are registration, labelling, and storage rules to follow.
sourceNotes: Food Standards Agency, Egg Marketing Regulations: Guidance for Small Producers (England, 2022). APHA, Poultry Registration Guidance (2023). Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Selling eggs guidance (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: The requirement for poultry keepers with 50 or more birds to register with the Animal and Plant Health Agency. Keepers with fewer than 50 birds are exempt from formal registration but must still follow egg safety rules.
The best-before date on egg boxes. Eggs must be sold with a best-before date no more than 28 days from the date of lay.

content.text: The rules for selling eggs in England depend on whether you have more or fewer than 50 hens in your flock. This guide covers the under-50-hen route: direct sale to the final consumer at the farm gate, doorstep, or local market. Selling through a retailer or caterer involves additional requirements.
You do not need to formally register with APHA as an egg producer.
only becomes compulsory at 50 birds. However, you must still comply with food hygiene law.
Eggs must be clean and undamaged. Dirty or cracked eggs cannot legally be sold.
each box with a best-before date of 28 days from lay. Use a rubber stamp or write clearly on the box. You must also provide your name and address.

Eggs should be stored in cool, dry conditions before sale. Refrigeration is not legally required for unprocessed eggs sold direct-to-consumer in the UK, but consistent cool storage extends shelf life.

Egg boxes for direct farm-gate sale must show at minimum: the producer's name and address, the best-before date, and a storage instruction (e.g. 'store in a cool dry place'). The words 'Class A' and the egg size (S/M/L/XL) are required if you are selling by grade; for informal farm-gate sale they are recommended but not legally required for under-50-hen flocks.
Collect eggs daily and remove any that are cracked, dirty, or misshapen. Do not sell these.

Lightly brush off dry dirt with a dry brush. Do not wash eggs before sale: washing removes the cuticle, a natural antibacterial coating, and reduces shelf life. A consumer can wash an egg immediately before cracking it.
Pack small end down in clean, food-grade boxes. Do not reuse boxes from another farm without removing any existing labelling.

If your flock reaches 50 birds, you must register as an egg producer with APHA before selling. At 350 birds, the full egg marketing regulations apply including mandatory grading. Both registration thresholds apply per premises, not per species.

attrs.cue: Customers returning eggs with bloody or meat spots
attrs.cause: Blood or meat spots are natural inclusions in the egg; they do not indicate disease. More common in some breeds, and in older hens
attrs.fix: The egg is safe to eat; the spot can be lifted out with a spoon. If you want to reduce their frequency, try a different breed (hybrid layers typically have fewer spots than traditional breeds).

attrs.cue: Shells are very thin or shell-less eggs appearing
attrs.cause: Insufficient calcium in the diet, or a hen at the end of her laying season
attrs.fix: Ensure ad-lib oyster shell or limestone grit is always available alongside the main feed. Thin-shelled eggs cannot be sold.
